text: Winegrid - Problem: Winegrid's platform monitored wine production in real time through IoT sensors — a technically sophisticated product aimed at an industry with deeply specific operational workflows. The core problem wasn't visual: it was a misalignment between how the engineering team modeled the product and how winemakers actually think about their work. Most engineers had no direct experience with industrial wine production, and that gap was showing up in the information architecture. The platform was already live and being actively developed, which meant there was no opportunity to start over — only to course-correct in motion.

text: Winegrid - Feature Development: One of the more constrained design problems was the sensor scheduling interface. Users needed to set a daily reading frequency, subject to real technical limits: no more than once every 30 minutes, at equal intervals, with a configurable start time. Rather than expose those rules as form validation after the fact, the design enforced them through the affordance itself: a frequency slider constrained to valid values, paired with a visual scheduler showing all resulting readings, and a dynamically generated plain-language summary of the selection. The goal was zero-error input without requiring users to understand the underlying constraints. This was built and shipped in AngularJS.

text:
Banco de Tempo de Santa Maria da Feira - Challenges: One of the biggest challenges was lining up with how they value this network. The value in belonging was not so much in obtaining services and saving money, as one might expect, although a lot of value could be obtained from here. Food, home maintenance services, tutoring, transportation, dance/yoga/painting classes etc... The main motivation was to be able to participate and underlyingly feel valued, and most times even just to have company. This makes sense as most of the more active members are retirees. This was possible to realize through questionnaires and also visits to the community with conversations over tea, getting to know if there was any community spirit, how some of them joined, some particular situations, and how the agency itself functions. The questionnaires aimed at understanding their motivations, current use of technology and foreseable usage of a digital platform for the Time Bank.

Another challenge was to establish the contribution that digital technologies might have to help them with their main problem: there's a higher tendency in members offering services than requiring them. Two conclusions were obtained in regard to this issue. The literary study established that changing the way their activity was framed by their internal and external discourse would make a significant difference. The empirical study established that a simple and familiar interface to choose and "purchase" services would motivate members to request more exchanges.

"If I need a ride somewhere, I don't request from the TimeBank, I take a cab." - a timebank participant
